bib.title: On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval", Orion Weller, Michael Boratko, Iftekhar Naim, Jinhyuk Lee (Google DeepMind, Johns Hopkins). ICLR 2026 (arXiv 2508.21038v2, 12 Mar 2026).

COVERAGE: Read the full 73,997 chars (all 23 pages): body, limitations, references skimmed, Appendices A-G including tables 2-7. Nothing skipped. Figures not extracted; only captions in text were read.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Theorem 1: for any embedding dimension d, some top-k subsets cannot be returned, and d needs to grow with log C(n,k).
 number: d >= log C(n,k) / log(1+1/gamma)
 setup: unit vectors, dot product, every k-subset must be realized with score margin 2*gamma; a lower bound only, gradient learning and tokenization ignored.
 quote: "Then n k ≤ (1 + 1/γ)^d, hence d ≥ log(n choose k) / log(1 + 1/γ)." Extracted as: "n\nk\n\n≤\n\n1 + 1γ d,henced≥ log  nklog 1 + 1/γ ."
 where: p.4, Sec 3
2. Table 1 (gamma=0.1) gives bounds that are small for k=2 and grow with k.
 number: k=2: 4 (n=100) up to 21 (n=10^11); k=100: 135 (n=1000), 329 (n=10^5), 905 (n=10^11); k=1000: 1354 (n=10^4), 8098 (n=10^11)
 setup: gamma=0.1, 2*gamma=0.2 score gap, "approximately standard for models based on empirical usage".
 quote: "We see for large k and n values these dimension requirements are already greater than those currently used for web-scale search."
 where: p.4, Table 1
3. Web-scale embeddings are truncated or quantized below 1k dims; research maximum is about 4096.
 number: <1k; 4096
 quote: "most embeddings used for web-scale search are quantized or truncated (e.g. through Matryoshka embeddings (Kusupati et al., 2022)) to less than 1k dimensions, while the largest embeddings used in research are around 4096"
 where: p.5
4. Best-case "free embedding" test: vectors optimized directly on the test qrels (k=2) fail past a critical n, and the critical n fits a cubic in d.
 number: y = -10.5322 + 4.0309d + 0.0520d^2 + 0.0037d^3, r2=0.999. Extrapolated critical n: 500k (d=512), 1.7m (768), 4m (1024), 107m (3072), 250m (4096). Measured: d=4 -> 10, d=12 -> 47, d=20 -> 120, d=45 -> 626.
 setup: random unit vectors, all C(n,k) queries, Adam, full-batch InfoNCE, early stop after 1000 iterations without improvement, n raised until 100% accuracy is lost. Only d=4 to 45 measured; larger d is extrapolated.
 quote: "Extrapolating this curve outward gives the critical-n values (for embedding size): 500k (512), 1.7m (768), 4m (1024), 107m (3072), 250m (4096)."
 where: p.6 and Table 6 (p.23)
5. The theoretical bound is far below what optimization needs.
 number: bound 4 at n=100 vs free embeddings needing d>18 (4.5x)
 quote: "Table 1 shows a lower bound of 4 for n= 100 whereas we see the free embeddings needing d >18 (e.g. a 4.5 multiplier even in the no-generalization or natural language case)."
 where: p.6
6. Authors conclude that even ideal test-set optimization at the largest dimensions cannot cover web-scale corpora.
 quote: "these numbers already show that for web-scale search, even the largest embedding dimensions with ideal test-set optimization are not enough to model all combinations."
 where: p.6
7. LIMIT (50k docs, 1000 queries, k=2, "who likes X") defeats SOTA single-vector models.
 number: full LIMIT Recall@100 at the highest dimension: Promptriever 18.9, GritLM 12.9 (4096), Gemini 10.0 (3072), E5-Mistral 8.3, Qwen3 4.8, Snowflake Arctic 3.3. Recall@2 is at most 3.2 (Promptriever 2048). BM25 gets 85.7/90.4/93.6 (R@2/10/100); GTE-ModernColBERT gets 23.1/34.6/54.8.
 setup: 46 relevant docs give C(46,2)=1035 queries; 49.95k extra non-relevant docs; docs about 100 tokens; MTEB framework; Gemini 2.5 Pro generated the attribute list (1850 items).
 quote: "in the full setting models struggle to reach even 20% recall@100 and in the 46 document version models cannot solve the task even with recall@20."
 where: p.8, Table 5 (p.22)
8. LIMIT-small (46 docs) is still unsolved by single-vector models.
 number: R@2 / R@10 / R@20 at the largest dimension: Promptriever 54.3/90.0/97.7, GritLM 38.4/75.4/90.5, E5-Mistral 29.5/68.1/85.2, Qwen3 19.0/52.3/73.8, Snowflake 19.4/54.9/76.0. BM25 97.8/100/100. ColBERT 83.5/97.6/99.1. Gemini Embed at 3072 gets 33.7/72.4/87.9.
 quote: "Despite having just 46 documents, models struggle even with recall@10 and cannot solve the task even with recall@20."
 where: Fig 4, Table 4 (p.21)
9. Performance rises with embedding dimension.
 number: e.g. E5-Mistral R@2 on small: 7.9 (d=32) to 29.5 (d=4096). Gemini R@10 on small: 23.0 (d=2) to 72.4 (d=3072). Snowflake plateaus at 19.4 from 1024 up, apparently because its native dimension is 1024.
 quote: "We also see that the dimensionality of the model is a limiting factor and that as the dimension increases, so does performance."
 where: Fig 3, Table 4
10. Not domain shift: fine-tuning on a LIMIT train split barely helps, while training on the test split solves it.
 number: train split R@10 rises from near 0 to at most 2.8 (R@100 up to 11.2 at d=1024). Test-split training gives R@2 85.5 to 96.5 (d=32 to 1024).
 setup: lightonai/modernbert-embed-large, full-dataset in-batch negatives, lr 5e-5, 5 epochs, projection to the target dimension (not MRL).
 quote: "Figure 5 shows the model trained on the training set cannot solve the problem, although it does see very minor improvement from near zero recall@10 to up to 2.8 recall@10."
 where: p.8, Table 3
11. Real models are well below the free-embedding bounds. The small version needs only 12 dims in free-embedding optimization, yet models with 64 dims fine-tuned on the test set still do not fully solve it.
 quote: "it is possible to overfit to the N= 46 version with only 12 dimensions. However, it is notable that the real models with 64 dimensions still cannot completely solve the task"
 where: p.9
12. Lexical models are not a panacea. With synonyms replacing the lexical overlap, BM25 collapses.
 number: BM25 R@2 on LIMIT-small falls from 97.8 to 10.6 (a drop of more than 89%). Qwen3 drops 38.9%. Per Fig 6, GTE-ColBERT falls 83.5 to 25.6.
 setup: Gemini 2.5 Pro synonyms (scientific names, similar meanings, hypernyms); some overlap remains (e.g. "Scuba Diving" -> "Underwater Diving").
 quote: "BM25 drops more than 89% whereas Qwen3 embedding drops 38.9%"
 where: p.9, Fig 6
 note: the Fig 6 number-to-model mapping is read from the extracted values and is partly ambiguous.
13. A long-context LLM reranker solves LIMIT-small, so cross-encoder style models do not share the dimension limit.
 number: 100% of 1000 queries
 setup: Gemini-2.5-Pro given all 46 docs and all 1000 queries in one generation.
 quote: "We find that it can successfully solve (100%) all 1000 queries in one forward pass."
 where: p.9
14. Sparse models behave as very high-dimensional single vectors, so they scale to more combinations. Multi-vector (ColBERT-style, MaxSim) scores far above dense but is not solved.
 quote: "Sparse models (both lexical and neural) can be thought of as single vectors but with very high dimensionality."
 where: p.10
15. Existing benchmarks cover a tiny part of the qrel combination space.
 number: QUEST has 325k docs, 20 relevant per query, 3357 queries; C(325k,20) = 7.1e+91. 50k docs with k=100 gives 7.7e+311 combinations.
 quote: "Thus, the 3k queries in QUEST can only cover an infinitesimally small part of the qrel combination space."
 where: p.6
16. LIMIT qrel graphs are far denser than standard IR sets.
 number: graph density 0.085481 vs 0.025641 (FollowIR Core17), 0.001449 (SciFact), 0.000037 (HotpotQA), 0 (NQ). Average query strength 28.4653 vs 0.5912, 0.4222, 0.1104, 0.
 quote: "LIMIT has significantly higher values for both of these metrics (i.e. 28 for query similarity compared to 0.6 or lower for the others)."
 where: App F, Table 2
17. Weak correlation between BEIR and LIMIT.
 number: BEIR vs LIMIT R@100: Snowflake 55.22 vs 3.3, Promptriever 56.40 vs 18.9, E5-Mistral 57.07 vs 8.3, GritLM 57.40 vs 12.9, Gemini 62.65 vs 10.0, Qwen3 62.76 vs 4.8
 quote: "We see that performance is generally not correlated"
 where: App D.4, Table 7
18. Sign-rank result from the first version (no margin). Any qrel matrix has sign-rank at most 2k, where k is the most relevant documents for one query. This is weaker than Theorem 1 and needs infinite precision.
 quote: "any qrel matrix has sign-rank at most 2k, where k is the largest number of documents for a particular query."
 where: App D.3

LIMITS (as the authors concede)
- Single-vector only. Results do not necessarily hold for multi-vector models, and the theory is not extended to them.
- No bound for a setting that tolerates some mistakes (capturing only a majority of the combinations).
- Cannot say which kinds of combinations fail, so some instruction or reasoning tasks may be solved perfectly.
- The bound is an "extreme lower bound". It depends on the margin gamma (0.1 chosen as typical, not measured).
- The free-embedding curve is extrapolated from d up to 45 (n up to 626) and only for k=2. The extrapolation to 4096 is a polynomial fit.
- Sigmoid loss (Bangachev et al. 2025) can solve free embeddings in fewer dimensions with no margin, so learnability is an open question (App C).
- LIMIT is synthetic: attribute-liking documents with an artificial dense qrel structure, English text only. The synonym set was generated with an LLM.
- Retrieval here is exhaustive scoring. The paper says nothing about ANN indexes (HNSW, IVF, PQ), so it does not show ANN-induced recall loss. Its relevance to the vector-database note is as a ceiling on what embedding dimension and top-k can represent, separate from index approximation.
- The paper's own advice: dense retrieval is still "useful for first stage results", with rerankers, multi-vector or sparse models added. No fix is given.

BUILDS ON
Clarkson 1988 and order-k Voronoi (Lee 1982; Bohler et al. 2015); Alon, Frankl, Rodl 1985 (sign rank); Vershynin 2018 and Conway et al. 1999 (sphere packing); Johnson-Lindenstrauss 1984; Reimers & Gurevych 2020 ("curse of dense low-dimensional IR for large index sizes"); Kusupati et al. 2022 (Matryoshka); Khattab & Zaharia 2020 (ColBERT); Oord et al. 2018 (InfoNCE); Kingma & Ba 2014 (Adam); Bangachev et al. 2025 (concurrent work); Ben-David et al. 2002.

CODE: none. Code and data are at https://github.com/google-deepmind/limit.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): LIMIT construction. All C(N,k) relevance combinations are mapped to "who likes X" queries over short person documents. It explains the dataset faster than prose.
- Fig 2 (p.6): critical-n against d with the cubic fit.
- Fig 3 (p.7): full LIMIT, recall against embedding dimension for 8 models.
- Fig 4 (p.8): LIMIT-small.
- Fig 5 (p.8): train-split vs test-split fine-tuning, which shows the failure is not domain shift.
- Fig 6 (p.9): LIMIT-small against the synonym variant.
- Fig 7 (p.18): BEIR vs LIMIT scatter.
I did not run the caption script. The captions are from the extracted text.
